The crisis starts before the streets

In Plain Sight

The numbers are clear. Youth homelessness often begins before adulthood. The timing, government spending, care-system pathways, and housing pressures show why prevention and earlier intervention matters.

This page presents the scale and timing of the problem; the full prevention solution is under What Works.
20%

of emergency-shelter users in Canada are youth aged 13 to 24. (ESDC, 2017)

40,000+

young people are estimated to be experiencing homelessness in Canada over the course of this year. (Homeless Hub, n.d.)

46%

Nearly half of chronically homeless adults first experienced homelessness before turning 25. (Homeless Hub, 2025)

1 in 3

More than one-third of youth placed by child protection services experienced homelessness in the first years following placement. (Goyette et al., 2024)

330+ million

At least 330 million people are experiencing homelessness worldwide, according to UN figures reiterated in July 2026. (UN-Habitat, 2026)

40.1%

About 40% of participating youth first experienced homelessness before the age of 16. (Gaetz et al., 2016)

15.7

The average age of first leaving home was 15.7, during the secondary-school years. (Gaetz et al., 2016)

57.8%

Over half of participating youth reported previous involvement with child-protection services. (Nichols et al., 2017)

16.7%

In 2023, 75 of 449 Canadian communities with emergency shelter services reportedly had youth-specific services. (Gaetz, 2026)

1 in 4

Only 24.8% of young people leaving care in Quebec had graduated from secondary school by age 19. (Goyette et al., 2020)

1 in 4

One in four Montreal renters reported difficulty paying rent in 2025. (Léger & Vivre en Ville, 2026)

~$800

is the average cost per youth participant receiving Upstream support for a year. That is not a lot to screen students and save lives. (COH, 2025)

40%

The Geelong Project, a COSS-based upstream prevention model, has been reported to reduce youth homelessness by 40%. (CAEH, 2018)

$53,144

Depending on the study, homelessness-related services can cost approximately $53,144 to $95,284 per person annually. (AppEco, 2026; COH, 2025)

28.2%

of participating youth experiencing homelessness identified as members of racialized communities. (Gaetz et al., 2016)

30.6%

of participating homeless youth identified as Indigenous. (Gaetz et al., 2016)

25-40%

is the commonly estimated percentage of 2SLGBTQIA+ youth that make up the youth homelessness population within Canadian literature. (Abramovich et al., 2025)

Core implication

If homelessness often begins while young people are still school-aged, the problem cannot be understood only through shelters, housing systems, or adult crisis services.

Youth homelessness starts earlier than many people think

Young people may still be attending school while experiencing hidden homelessness, family violence, housing instability, poverty, untreated distress, or difficult transitions out of care. They may not yet use homelessness services. They may not identify as homeless. They may not tell an adult what is happening.

Child protection, mental health, and service gaps

Youth homelessness is deeply connected to child protection, mental health, and service-system gaps. The statistics above show that many young people are already known to public systems before homelessness becomes visible. The moral and policy problem is not that no one ever saw them. It is that seeing did not always become coordinated support.

Why schools appear in the data

Schools are one of the few systems that have consistent contact with young people during the period when homelessness risk often first appears. Absenteeism, exhaustion, hunger, withdrawal, behavioural changes, academic decline, instability, and disconnection can all appear in school before a young person enters a formal crisis system.
